question: Why is positional encoding important in transformers?
rewritten_query: Why is positional encoding important in transformers?
answer: Positional encoding is important because attention is positionally independent—it uses inner products, so shuffling token positions would produce the same attention without position information. Adding a position embedding gives the transformer a sense of order in the sequence [1] (timestamp=1881.9s). This is why transformers are said to lack positional dependence, so a position embedding (e.g., sines and cosines) is added to encode position [3] (timestamp=100.3s).

question: How does attention relate sequence length to compute?
rewritten_query: How does attention relate sequence length to compute?
answer: Attention is quadratic in sequence length: “attention is n squared and … where n is a sequence length and that gets really expensive” [3] (timestamp=1825.8s). This means compute grows with the square of sequence length, so “you want to make sure the sent sequence is shorter” because “attention is quadratic” [4] (timestamp=4068.6s). More generally, the total arithmetic operations are “order of magnitude batch size sequence length hidden dim squared,” with a softmax cost that has “an N squared component” [2] (timestamp=4558.3s). Thus, longer sequences cause attention compute to scale quadratically, motivating methods to reduce attention computation [3] (timestamp=1825.8s).

question: How do you handle out-of-vocabulary words in tokenization?

answer: Out-of-vocabulary words are handled by training the tokenizer on raw text to build a vocabulary tailored to the data, so that rare sequences are split into smaller units instead of using an “unk” token [1] (timestamp=4347.9s). The context notes that people used to assign an “unk” token for unseen words, but that is described as “really ugly” and can mess up perplexity calculations [2] (timestamp=4285.1s). This is achieved with byte pair encoding (BPE), which breaks input into frequently occurring chunks and can split rare sequences into multiple tokens [1] (timestamp=4347.9s) [3] (timestamp=1701.2s).

question: What is the difference between a tokenizer vocabulary and a merge list?
rewritten_query: What is the difference between a tokenizer vocabulary and a merge list (BPE merges, subword tokenization rules, wordpiece vocabularies, token dictionaries, byte-pair encoding merges)?
answer: A tokenizer vocabulary is a mapping from token IDs (integers) to their byte representations, i.e., the actual set of tokens the tokenizer can output [1]. A merge list is an ordered list of byte-pair tuples `(<token1>, <token2>)` representing which tokens were merged together, in creation order, to build the BPE tokenizer [1]. In BPE, the merge list defines the steps used to combine frequent byte chunks into larger tokens, while the vocabulary contains the resulting tokens [2][5].

question: What happens during the backward pass in training?
rewritten_query: What occurs during the backward pass (backpropagation, reverse mode, gradient computation phase) in neural network training?
answer:
During the backward pass, gradients propagate back through the network using activations that were stored during the forward pass. As described, you “go forwards up on the tree and keep track of activations,” then “when I go backwards, I’m going to use the activations that I stored to compute the backwards signal down my tree” [3] (timestamp=3008.8s). From a systems perspective, the backward pass consumes these stored activations, e.g., intermediate outputs from operations like sigmoid, to compute gradients [4] (timestamp=3040.3s). Also, the backward pass can include recomputation, such as in FlashAttention, which “has the recomputation piece as well” [5] (timestamp=4629.4s).

In terms of architecture, gradient propagation is made simpler and more stable when the residual stream is kept clean: on the pre-norm side, the input “X propagates all the way up to the top,” and “that allows gradients to propagate if you in the backward pass straight through this,” which “makes gradient propagation very simple, which improves both stability and signal propagation” [2] (timestamp=660.3s). Similarly, with pre-norm and careful initialization, “the gradient size is kind of remains the same” because of “nice straight through propagation in the backward pass,” whereas post-layer-norm creates “complicated effects” that change gradient norms as you go backward [1] (timestamp=691.6s).
